h: What to expect at the bottom of the shaft
p: Going underground starts with the cage, the lift that carried miners down the shaft for generations. You'll drop around ninety metres into the hillside, then follow your guide through the old roadways and workings. Everyone gets a helmet, a cap lamp and a battery belt, and it's a genuine thrill when the lights go off for a moment and you realise just how dark a pit really is.

A few things are worth knowing in advance. Anything with a battery, like phones, watches, car keys with electronic fobs and cameras, has to be left on the surface, because of the risk of sparks underground. That means no selfies down there, so soak it up instead. It's cool and can be damp underground even in summer, so bring a jumper and wear sturdy, closed-in shoes.

Look out for the underground stables, where pit ponies were kept. Their stories are often among the moments that stick with kids most. Back up top, the mining galleries show how coal was worked in more recent decades, a big contrast to the older tunnels you've just walked through.
Allow at least half a day for the underground tour plus the surface buildings.

The landscape around Blaenavon is part of the attraction, and it's been a World Heritage Site since 2000. Up on the Blorenge mountain, Keepers Pond is a cracking spot for a picnic with huge views. Head a bit further and the market town of Abergavenny makes a good base, with the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park, the area long known as the Brecon Beacons, right on the doorstep.
